content: The abdomen is the anatomical region of the body located between the chest (thorax) and the thighs (pelvis). It houses several vital organs, including the ureters, intestines, liver, anus, bladder, gallbladder, and components of the reproductive system, excluding the breast. This region is also commonly referred to as the belly or venter. In humans and many other vertebrates, the abdomen is the area between the thoracic cavity and the pelvic cavity, separated by the thoracic diaphragm. In fully developed insects, the abdomen constitutes the third or posterior segment of the body, following the head and thorax. In vertebrates, the abdomen contains critical components of the digestive system, such as the gallbladder, liver, anus, appendix, rectum, and intestines. It also includes parts of the urinary system, such as the ureters, bladder, and urethra. Additionally, the internal reproductive organs are located in the abdomen. In females, these include the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, vulva, and vagina, while in males, they include the testes, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, penis, and urethra. The abdomen also contains some of the largest and most accessible blood vessels, making it a common site for medical procedures like catheterization. In many animals, the abdomen is often distinct in coloration from the rest of the body. In species with fur or hair, the abdomen is frequently hairless or nearly so. Structurally, the abdomen is oval-shaped and represents the largest cavity in the body. It can be divided into the upper and lower extremities. The lower extremity encompasses the inner surface of the bony pelvis, while the upper extremity is formed by the diaphragm, which acts as a dome over the abdomen and extends to the upper border of the fifth rib. In invertebrates, the abdomen is composed of a series of concave upper plates called tergites and convex lower plates called sternites, all held together by a tough yet flexible membrane. The abdomen in insects contains the digestive tract and reproductive organs. It typically consists of eleven segments in most insect orders, although the eleventh segment is absent in the adult forms of many higher orders. The number of visible segments varies among species, with some, like the common honeybee, having only seven visible segments. In springtails (Collembola), the abdomen has only six segments. Unlike other arthropods, adult insects lack legs on their abdomen. However, some exceptions exist, such as Protura, which have rudimentary leg-like appendages on the first three abdominal segments, and Archaeognatha, which possess small articulated structures called styli that are sometimes considered vestigial appendages. Many larval insects, including those in the Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) and Symphyta (sawflies), have fleshy appendages called prolegs on their abdominal segments. These prolegs, in addition to their thoracic legs, help them grip the edges of plant leaves as they move.
